paragraphs.text: Date of hearing. 14.10.2026 Appellant by: Mr. Muhammad Yaqoob Sidhu, Advocate. State by: Mr. Abdul Jabbar Dogar, D.P.G. Complainant by Nemo Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz, J.: - Mansoob Ahmad Shah (appellant) was tried in case FIR No.36, dated 07.09.2013, registered under section 409 of Pakistan Penal Code, 1860 (“PPC”) read with section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 (“PCA”), at Police Station, Anti- Corruption Establishment (“ACE”) Pakpattan Sharif, by the learned Special Judge, Anti-Corruption Court, Camp at Pakpattan. The learned Trial Court, after conclusion of the trial, vide judgment dated 12.04.2018 (“Impugned Judgment”), convicted and sentenced the appellant as under: -  Under section 409 PPC to undergo 03-years R.I. with a fine of Rs.50,000/- and, in default thereof, to further undergo simple imprisonment for 03 months;  Under section 5(2)47 of PCA to undergo 03-years R.I. with a fine of Rs.50,000/- and, in default thereof, to further undergo simple imprisonment for 03 months.  Under section 9 of the Pakistan Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958, he was also sentenced to a fine of Rs.83,335/- and, in default thereof, to further undergo simple imprisonment for three months. All the sentences of imprisonment were ordered to run concurrently. He was also extended the benefit of section 382-B of Criminal Procedure Code, 1898 (“Cr.P.C.”). Feeling aggrieved by the said convictions and sentences, the appellant filed instant criminal appeal before this Court.

Succinctly stated, the facts of the case, as detailed in para No.1 of the impugned judgment, are as under: - “Briefly stated facts relating to instant case are that complainant (Muhammad Afzal) (PW-1) moved an application (Exh PA) against accused Mehboob Ahmad by alleging that he while acting as Civil Nazir, being a public servant, received an amount of Rs.150,000/- which was handed over to him by successful bidder namely Muhammad Shameer.”

After registration of case, appellant was arrested and investigated, and challan was sent to the learned trial Court. After receipt of challan and fulfilment of procedural requirements, appellant was charge-sheeted, to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial. The prosecution was asked to produce its witnesses before the learned trial Court, whereupon the prosecution produced six witnesses. After the closure of prosecution evidence, the statement of appellant under section 342 Cr.P.C. was recorded by trial court, wherein he refuted the allegations levelled against him and professed his innocence. He, however, neither opted to appear as his own witness on oath as provided under section 340(2) of the Cr. P.C. in disproof of allegations levelled against him, nor produced any evidence in his defence.

The principal question requiring determination is whether prosecution succeeded in proving essential ingredients of criminal breach of trust under section 409 PPC. For attracting the said provision, prosecution must establish entrustment of property, or dominion over it, to appellant in relevant capacity and dishonest misappropriation, conversion, use or disposal thereof in violation of obligation governing such entrustment [1]. An examination of the offences set out in Chapter XVII of PPC. under the heading “Of Criminal Breach of Trust” reveals that the expression “trust” appears in every provision and forms the basis and cornerstone of each of them. Since “entrustment” is one of the foundational elements of the offence, its meaning requires elaboration, however, the expression “entrusted” has not been defined in PPC. Section 405 PPC speaks of a person “being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property”. The words “in any manner” enlarge the modes by which entrustment may be made; they do not dispense with proof of the entrustment itself. Entrustment does not contemplate the creation of a trust with all the technicalities of the law of trust. It contemplates a relationship whereby the owner of property, or a person lawfully entitled to deal with it, makes it over to another for a specified purpose, the transferor remaining its owner and the transferee acquiring only its custody, to be held and applied for that purpose alone. The Supreme Court of Pakistan has held that an entrustment exists when possession of property is temporarily given to a recipient, whereupon a fiduciary relationship arises between the giver and the recipient, and that there is no entrustment in transactions such as investments, loans, sales or promises of profit [2]. This interpretation vividly refers to the following effects: - i. that the entrustment is a question, whose establishment requires the production of positive evidence, for which the prosecution must show who made over the property, to whom, when and for what purpose. [1] Dr Waqar Hameed v. The State and another (2026 SCP 233), Abdul Rashid Nasir and others v. The State (2009 S C M R 517) [2] Ayesha Tayyab v. Station House Officer, Police Station Cantt, District Sialkot, etc.‟ (2025 SCMR 1117), at para 5, relying upon „Shahid Imran v. The State‟ (2011 SCMR 1614) and „Muhammad Ali v. Mst. Samina Qasim Tarar‟ (2022 SCMR 2001)). ii. where the accused is a public servant, the entrustment or dominion must have been conferred upon him in, and by reason of, his official capacity. It is not enough that he held an office which, in ordinary course, might have brought such property under his control; it must further be shown that his dominion over the particular property was the result of entrustment. iii. the “dominion” contemplated by section 405 PPC means actual control over the specific property, not a general supervisory authority over an office or its records. When these principles are applied to prosecution evidence, it comes to light that the complainant (PW-1) conceded that Zar-e-soem in pre- emption suits is to be deposited in the National Bank through Challan Form 32-A by the plaintiff himself; the law, therefore, did not contemplate that such money would pass through the hands of Nazir. The successful bidder (PW-2) stated that he paid Rs.150,000/- to the court auctioneer, Ch. Khadim Hussain Advocate, in the appellant‟s absence, and never deposited the amount with appellant. Neither the court auctioneer nor any other person who claims to have made over the money to appellant was produced. The foundational element of “entrustment” is, therefore, not established.

It is well settled that a criminal conviction cannot rest upon conjecture, surmise or assumption [3]. It follows that mere suspicion, whether arising from the recovery of documents or from the official position held by an accused, cannot substitute for proof of these essential ingredients. A careful appraisal of the evidence reveals that prosecution neither examined any person who allegedly entrusted the disputed amounts to appellant, nor does the record disclose who allegedly delivered the money to appellant. The evidence of these witnesses was the best evidence available to prosecution, yet it was withheld without any plausible explanation. Such withholding attracts the presumption under Article 129, illustration (g), of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984, [3] Dr Waqar Hameed‟s case, Supra (2026 SCP 233), para 7 (“QSO”) and an adverse inference may validly be drawn that their evidence, had it been produced, would not have supported the prosecution case [4].

This Court finds material contradictions in the statements of the PWs. Complainant Muhammad Afzal ACOC (PW-1), during cross- examination, stated that “It is correct that Zar-e-som of pre-emption suits is to be deposited in the National Bank through Challan Form 32-A by the plaintiff himself…. It is correct that disputed Challan Form 32-A is not signed or sealed by the accused…. I became complainant in this case on the direction of the Inquiry Officer but I was not a witness of the whole episode…. My entire evidence is based on hearsay as it was narrated by the plaintiff of the pre-emption suit. I cannot depose whether any amount was misappropriated or not by the accused.” In his cross-examination, the complainant unequivocally admitted that he was not a witness to the occurrence and that his entire evidence was based on what the plaintiff of the pre-emption suit had narrated to him. Such testimony, being admittedly hearsay, is inadmissible under Article 71 of the QSO, 1984. Hearsay evidence is the weakest kind of evidence; it carries no evidentiary value in the eye of law and cannot form the basis of a conviction on a criminal charge [5].

Muhammad Shameer (PW-2) stated that “The Court auctioneer was appointed on the order of the Civil Court and the name of court auctioneer was Ch. Khadim Hussain Advocate of Pakpattan…. I deposited the disputed amount 25% of the total auction money worth Rs.150,000/- to the said Court auctioneer namely Ch. Khadim Hussain Advocate at the spot of auction i.e. Chak No.56/D. It is correct that Nazir/accused Mansoob Shah was not present over their when I deposited the disputed amount of Rs.150,000/- to Ch. Khadam Hussain Advocate. I never deposited the said amount with the accused Mansoob Shah.” The evidence of this witness is fatal to prosecution case. The [4] Amjad Ali v. The State (2026 S C M R 729), Abdul Qadeer v. The State (2024 SCMR 1146), and Riasat Ali v. The State (2024 SCMR 1224) [5] Sajjan Solangi v. The State (2019 SCMR 872) application (Exh.PA), on which the case was registered, alleged that the amount of Rs.150,000/- had been handed over to appellant by this very witness. In the witness-box, however, PW-2 stated that he paid the amount to the court auctioneer, Ch. Khadim Hussain Advocate, at the site of the auction, that the appellant was not present at that time, and that he never deposited the amount with the appellant. The only witness of the alleged payment has thus disowned the very entrustment on which the charge rests. If the money was paid to the court auctioneer, it was for the prosecution to show, through the auctioneer or the record of the Civil Court, that it was subsequently made over to appellant in his capacity as Nazir. No such evidence was led. The court auctioneer, who alone could have spoken to that fact, was not produced, and the adverse inference under Article 129, illustration (g), of the QSO, 1984, as discussed above, applies.

Muhammad Hasnat Shabbir (PW-3), during cross-examination, stated that “The disputed money was being received by both Nazir namely Muhammad Ramzan and Mansoob Shah. I do not know that who of the said accused persons had received the disputed amount.” It is pertinent to mention here that co-accused Muhammad Ramzan passed away during the trial. The statement of Muhammad Hasnat Shabbir (PW- 3) does not cure this defect. He deposed that the disputed money was being received by two Nazirs, namely Muhammad Ramzan and appellant, and conceded that he did not know which of them had received the disputed amount. Evidence that leaves it open whether the property was entrusted to appellant or to another official does not prove entrustment to appellant; at best, it casts suspicion upon both, and suspicion cannot take the place of proof; however grave or strong, it can never be a proper substitute for the standard of proof required in a criminal case [6]. The death of co-accused Muhammad Ramzan during the trial does not relieve prosecution of its burden of proving, by positive evidence, that the money in question came into the hands of appellant. A cumulative assessment of [6] Mst. Asia Bibi v. The State and other (P L D 2019 SC 64), Muhammad Ashraf v. The State (2016 S C M R 1617), and Muhammad Jamshaid and another v. The State and others (2016 S C M R 1019) the statements of PW-1, PW-2 and PW-3 reveal that they are mutually inconsistent: the application (Exh.PA) attributes direct receipt of the money to appellant, PW-2 attributes its receipt to the court auctioneer, and PW-3 is unable to attribute its receipt to either Nazir. These are the material contradictions referred to above, and they go to the root of the alleged entrustment

Ghazanfar Tufail (PW-4), the Investigating Officer, in his cross- examination stated that “I did not verify the veracity of allegation contained in the FIR from NBP Pakpattan Sharif regarding the deposit of disputed amount. It is correct that no recovery was effected from the accused during investigation…..I did not require the accused Mansoob Shah for obtaining his specimen writing and specimen signatures for their comparison with the disputed receipts and other documents concerned in this case. It is correct that I am not in a position to depose about the preparation of disputed receipts that whether these were prepared by the accused Mansoob Shah. It is correct that disputed receipts was not taken into possession by me nor the same was produced to me during investigation……It is correct that I could not said Muhammad Shameer to prove his version by producing other corroborative evidence and witnesses.” The admissions of the Investigating Officer (PW-4) show that the investigation was perfunctory on every point that mattered. He did not verify from the National Bank of Pakistan whether the disputed amount had been deposited, although that was the one inquiry capable of establishing whether any public money was in fact lost. He did not obtain the appellant‟s specimen writing or signatures, and he conceded that he could not say whether the disputed receipts were prepared by appellant. He further admitted that the disputed receipts were neither taken into his possession nor produced before him during the investigation, so their custody and integrity, from their alleged recovery until their production in Court, remain unaccounted for. Nor did he require PW-2 to substantiate his version through corroborative evidence. The prosecution thus failed to collect the very evidence that could have connected appellant with the alleged loss. The consequences of these omissions must fall upon prosecution, which bears the burden of proof under Article 117 of the QSO, 1984, and not upon the accused.

These circumstances create a substantial gap/doubt in prosecution evidence concerning the alleged entrustment to appellant. The allegation of misappropriation is equally unsupported by cogent evidence. Although the prosecution attributed a substantial financial loss, no recovery of the alleged amount was affected from appellant. The Investigating Officer admitted that no specimen of appellant‟s handwriting was obtained for comparison with the disputed register. He further acknowledged that no verification was obtained from the concerned bank regarding the genuineness of the disputed challan forms. The complainant admitted that he neither conducted an inquiry into their genuineness nor approached the concerned bank for verification. In the absence of reliable verification from the relevant bank, expert comparison of handwriting, or other dependable evidence establishing their fabrication and attribution to appellant, the allegation that the forms were forged cannot be accepted as proved [7].

The prosecution in this case was required to establish a reliable evidentiary connection between the appellant, the disputed documents and the alleged loss of public money. However, it relied merely upon the recovery of a private register with disputed challan forms from a room associated with the appellant, without proving appellant‟s possession or authorship of those documents, their authenticity, or their connection with any specific amount allegedly dishonestly appropriated by him; hence, the charge could not be established beyond reasonable doubt. The appellant‟s official position, by itself, cannot dispense with the prosecution‟s obligation to prove each essential ingredient of the offence charged.

It is a cardinal principle of criminal jurisprudence that prosecution must prove its case beyond reasonable doubt, and the accused is entitled to the benefit of every reasonable doubt emerging from the evidence. The gravity of offence does not dilute this standard; however serious the [7] See Articles 59, 78 and 84 of the Qanun-e-Shahadat Order, 1984 allegation, a court can do complete justice only by insisting on proof that meets it, and not by allowing the nature of the charge to supply what the evidence lacks [8]. This benefit is not a concession by way of grace but a right flowing from the prosecution‟s failure to discharge its burden. Presently, the deficiencies discussed above are not peripheral discrepancies; rather, they strike at the very basis of the charge. The evidence does not establish entrustment or dishonest misappropriation with any degree of certainty to sustain a conviction. In view of the above, the absence of any concrete evidence and the failure to establish the appellant‟s requisite intention under the relevant provisions cumulatively create reasonable doubt. In the case of „Tariq Pervez versus The State‟ (1995 SCMR 1345), the Hon‟ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, at page 1347, was pleased to observe as under: - „5……..The concept of benefit of doubt to an accused person is deep-rooted in our country. For giving him benefit of doubt, it is not necessary that there should be many circumstances creating doubts. If there is a circumstance which creates reasonable doubt in a prudent mind about the guilt of the accused, then the accused will be entitled to the benefit not as a matter of grace and concession but as a matter of right.‟ The Hon‟ble Supreme Court of Pakistan while reiterating the same principle in the case of „Muhammad Akram versus The State‟ (2009 SCMR 230), at page 236, observed as under: - „13……..It is an axiomatic principle of law that in case of doubt, the benefit thereof must accrue in favour of the accused as a matter of right and not of grace. It was observed by this Court in the case of Tariq Pervez v. The State 1995 SCMR 1345 that for giving the benefit of doubt, it was not necessary that there should be many circumstances creating doubts. If there is circumstance which created reasonable doubt in a prudent mind about the guilt of the [8] Najaf Ali Shah versus The State‟ (2021 SCMR 736), and Muhammad Mansha v. The State (2018 SCMR 772) accused, then the accused would be entitled to the benefit of doubt not as a matter of grace and concession but as a matter of right.‟

For the foregoing reasons, this Court is of the considered view that the learned trial court did not properly appreciate the material deficiencies in the prosecution evidence; consequently, Criminal Appeal No.210897 of 2018 is allowed. The judgment dated 12.04.2018 passed by learned Special Judge, Anti-Corruption, camp at Pakpattan Sharif, is set aside and appellant is acquitted of the charges. He is on bail; his bail bonds stand discharged and the surety is relieved of his obligation. (Khalid Ibn-i-Aziz) JUDGE Approved for Reporting Judge Umar Hayat
